extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners interested in philosophy of science, logic, and the theory of induction (e.g., philosophers, scientists reflecting on method)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for forming and assessing inductive generalizations and for characterizing laws of nature; i.e., how to infer universal propositions from observed instances and how to judge their strength and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called is Generalization from Experience: inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which 'resemble' the former in what are regarded as the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction consists in inferring universality from observed particular cases that resemble one another in relevant (material) circumstances; selecting which circumstances are material is critical to the validity of the generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Uniformity of Nature (ultimate major premise)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are such things in nature as parallel cases; that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again — i.e. the course of nature is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal principle is the ultimate major premise of all inductions: it does not itself prove individual inductions but is a necessary condition for induction to be proved. Poincaré also emphasizes that this axiom is itself an induction, arrived at only after many particular generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity in material circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction infers that a phenomenon occurring in observed instances will occur in all instances that 'resemble' the former in the material circumstances; the distinction between material and immaterial circumstances must be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining which circumstances are material (relevant) vs immaterial (irrelevant) is essential and often the central difficulty of forming a sound induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden major premise / induction as suppressed syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction may be thrown into the form of a syllogism by supplying a major premise (the general principle), i.e. inductions are syllogisms with the major suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the implicit general principle (major premise) underlying an inductive inference; identifying it clarifies the grounds and exposes whether one is relying on the uniformity axiom or another generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction by simple enumeration ('inductio per enumerationem simplicem') is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of ascribing general truth to propositions true in every instance we happen to know of (simple enumeration without seeking contradictory instances) is a weak and often defective form of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying only on the unsearched-for, presented cases (mere palpatio) creates vulnerable generalizations; scientific method requires active search for counterinstances and controlled inquiry rather than passive accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of seeking contrary instances / interrogating nature (Baconian experimentalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding a universal proposition from absence of counterinstances, one must have reason to believe that if contrary instances existed, we should have known of them — hence the importance of searching, experimenting, and 'interrogating' nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation and deliberate inquiry to look for contradictory evidence are crucial; unprompted acceptance of presented instances is inadequate for strong inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample representativeness / evidential sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: To be justified in concluding universal truth from observed instances, we must have grounds to believe that the absence of known exceptions is not merely due to lack of observation (i.e., that the sample observed is representative or that contrary cases would have been observed if they existed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement explains why identical quantities of observed instances can justify different degrees of confidence depending on whether the domain is one where exceptions would likely have been detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-specific reliability of uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of an induction depends on the class of phenomena: some classes (e.g., general anatomy or certain physical properties) exhibit much greater constancy than others (e.g., animal coloration), so identical empirical evidence yields different credibility across classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the case belongs to a class known from experience to show high constancy; if so, fewer instances (sometimes a single well-founded one) may suffice for a firm induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-instance sufficiency in high-regularity domains
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain domains where uniformities are extremely reliable (e.g., some physical laws or carefully controlled chemical results), a single well-executed instance may justify a universal proposition — 'a universal proposition from a singular one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is legitimate only when the case belongs to a class in which experience has shown near-absolute uniformity; verify that the experiment was properly conducted rather than demand repetition for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger inductions as touchstones for weaker ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions that are better established (stronger) serve as tests and foundations for weaker inductions; weaker inductions may be elevated in certainty if they can be deduced from stronger ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to relate proposed generalizations to more general, better-established uniformities; derivability from such laws confers additional certainty and can convert a provisional induction into a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency among inductions and mutual testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions connected by ratiocination confirm each other; inductions that yield deductive consequences incompatible with stronger inductions indicate that one or the other must be revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive relations between generalizations to test for mutual consistency; incompatible conclusions force re-evaluation or guarded expression of the conflicting inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature as the simplest independent uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature are the separate uniformities reduced to their most simple expression: the fewest and simplest assumptions from which the existing order of nature could be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer generalizations that explain many phenomena by positing fewer, simpler, and independent assumptions (parsimony/explanatory economy). Distinguish between primary laws and derivative 'results' that follow from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: law versus result (derivative uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex uniformities that are mere cases or consequences of simpler uniformities should be treated as results of laws rather than as independent laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a regularity can be deduced from simpler laws, regard it as a corollary; doing so clarifies theory structure and concentrates explanation in the simplest independent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire for empirical verification even when deduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a complex uniformity can be deduced from simpler laws, 'verification by specific experience would still be desirable, and might possibly be indispensable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction from laws increases confidence, but independent empirical confirmation remains important to detect errors in premises, application, or hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental inquiry as method for 'unraveling the web' of uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of experimental inquiry are contrivances for unraveling the web of intermingled uniformities so that individual threads (separate laws) can be studied apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and methods to isolate phenomena and separate entangled causes/regularities rather than accepting composite appearances; experimental contrivances should aim to make independent threads manifest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method depends on prior reliable inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any scientific method of induction presupposes that some inductions deserving of reliance have already been made; it is impossible to start entirely afresh without assumed generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and critically examine the prior generalizations used as foundations; science advances by refining and sometimes revising these prior inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective hierarchy: revise weaker inductions when they conflict with stronger ones
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions, or with conclusions deductively derivable from them, then, unless the stronger ones are shown to be overstated, the weaker induction must give way or be more cautiously expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precedence to well-established generalizations when resolving conflicts; use the network of inductions to diagnose and correct overgeneralization or misapplied instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey of empirical regularities to determine where induction is trustworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine in what degree induction may be relied upon in particular kinds of cases, we must survey past inductions to know which sorts of uniformities have historically been invariable and which have varied with time, place, or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before depending on simple enumeration or limited observation, consult the broader empirical record about the class of phenomena to judge typical stability and thus the likely reliability of new generalizations.
